checkpoints: The port exposes neutral money operations (charge/createOrder, and refund where supported) taking amount as an integer in the smallest currency unit, currency, an internal intent/order id, and a reference/description string — nothing provider-specific appears in the types

What stays OUT of the port on purpose: computing the amount from the catalog, checking a webhook's transferAmount against the ledger, and every write to the ledger — all of that is the service's job so a provider swap can't bypass guards
Exactly one binding at the composition root decides which implementation (real vs mock) is wired in
The mock is deterministic (stable ids, no network) precisely so e2e tests and interviews don't need real credentials to exercise the whole flow

The honest asymmetry: the card provider's charge returns a result in the same round trip, while the QR provider's createOrder only returns a pending order and a QR — the actual paid transition arrives later via webhook, so the port models this as a different capability/return type rather than forcing a synchronous answer

Signature verification for the webhook is a separate, per-provider verifier contract living at the ingress, not a method on this port, because verifying an inbound callback and talking outbound to a provider are different responsibilities with different boundaries

The module boundary is a 5-step pipeline: ingress (raw body + signature header) → verifier port → parse → idempotency store (keyed by event id) → atomic apply (transition + mark-processed) → response mapper
The ingress/controller layer does exactly two things — preserves the raw body before parsing, and calls the verifier — and must not read the payload before the signature is known to be valid

The verifier is an abstract contract (e.g. verify({rawBody, signature, timestamp}): boolean) with two implementations — a deterministic mock HMAC and the provider's real verification — with exactly one DI binding picking which runs, keeping the downstream pipeline provider-agnostic and testable

JSON parsing happens only after verification passes, and the idempotency store is looked up by eventId BEFORE any ledger read, so a duplicate is short-circuited correctly even if the underlying ledger record later disappears
The ledger transition write and the mark-processed write must commit together — one transaction in a database, or one synchronous block with no await in between in the in-memory form

Splitting the two writes breaks under both orderings: mark-processed first then crash loses the event's effect permanently while the system believes it's done; apply the ledger first then crash before marking causes the redelivery to double-apply — and even without a crash, any timing gap between the writes is itself a race
The response mapper maps by outcome: new+verified → apply then 200; duplicate+verified → 200 with a duplicate flag; bad signature → 401; unparseable payload → 400; payment not found → 404

Exactly-once is not inherent to webhooks — it's manufactured from four pieces together: at-least-once delivery, keyed dedup, atomic apply, and an honest ack (a 2xx that genuinely means processed) — dropping any one collapses the guarantee

The confirm request arrives with the stale expectedAmount while the ledger has already been re-priced, so the amount-mismatch guard fires immediately and throws 400 BEFORE the gateway is ever called — no money moves
The ledger stays at requires_confirmation with no partial state written anywhere

On a correctly written client, processing is only a temporary optimistic guess made for a snappy UI, so when confirm errors out the catch branch must reconcile that guess to the truth (move it to failed and surface the error)

The classic bug is a catch branch that forgets to reconcile: the UI keeps showing processing forever even though the server rejected it long ago — a silent failure harder to catch than a loud on-screen exception, and it's the client's responsibility to prevent it
The correct recovery path is to recreate the intent at the new price and re-present the total for the user to re-approve, never silently retrying the old confirm at a figure the user never agreed to
expectedAmount exists specifically to serve stale-cart detection, not to let the client decide the price

The lifecycle is asymmetric: the actual transfer happens out-of-band inside the customer's banking app where the server is never present, so the server only learns money has arrived asynchronously through a confirmation webhook, never through any call from the client

The bridge between an anonymous sum of money and a specific order is the reference: at order-creation time the server computes the amount from the catalog and generates a unique reference, embedding it in the description shown with the QR — so the transfer note already carries that reference by the time the customer transfers
The webhook only carries the exact note the payer typed and has no idea of the internal order id, so the server itself must extract the reference token from that note
The server looks up the extracted reference in a reference index (a map of reference to orderId) to pin down exactly one order in the ledger

The client must never have a "mark myself as paid" API — if it did, anyone could skip the transfer and still unlock the order — so the client only polls and reflects the ledger's real status, never asserts it

When the reference can't be extracted or the extracted token isn't in the index (a mistyped note or bank truncation), the server must not guess which order the money belongs to — the event is ignored/logged for manual reconciliation and the order stays pending
Better an unmatched event than money misattributed to the wrong order

The internal ledger is an independent, auditable source of truth that records every status transition (e.g., requires_confirmation → succeeded/failed) the instant it happens, without needing to re-query the gateway.
Without a ledger, checking status means a round-trip to the gateway every single time.
Without a ledger, a late or duplicate webhook has nothing to compare against.
Without a ledger, period-end reconciliation has no internal figure to reconcile against the gateway's statement.
The system's guards — the amount-mismatch check at confirm time, the remaining-amount logic for refunds — are reads against the ledger, not calls to the gateway.
The honest cost is that ledger and gateway are two parallel sources of state that can drift out of sync.

That drift is accepted deliberately because having a ledger is precisely what makes reconciliation possible in the first place, to detect and compensate for it — treating the gateway as the sole source of truth wouldn't even allow drift to be detected, since nothing internal remains to compare against.
Conclusion: own your books, and let the gateway be nothing more than an integration.
Gateways deliver at-least-once and decide whether to keep retrying based on exactly one signal: they stop if and only if they see a 2xx status code.
A duplicate event is not an error — it's a valid retry of something already finished, so it must return 200 (with a duplicate flag for logging/observability) and must not re-apply the transition.
Returning an error on a valid duplicate makes the gateway read it as a failure and retry forever.

Genuine rejections keep honest HTTP semantics: 401 for a bad signature (rejected before the payload is even parsed, since the source isn't trusted yet), 400 for a malformed payload, and 404 for an event pointing at a payment that doesn't exist.
The system must never silently manufacture a junk record just to have something to answer with, even to give the 404 case something concrete to point at.
200 is itself a promise: sending it before the event is durably recorded means a crash in between loses the event permanently, since the gateway already got its 2xx and will never resend.
The mandatory ordering is verify signature -> check idempotency (dedup) -> apply and persist -> only then return 200.

'Exactly-once processing' is not natural — it's the result of pairing the gateway's at-least-once delivery with idempotent application on the server; dropping either half breaks the contract at one of the two extremes.
The reconciliation report is deliberately read-only — that is the whole point, not an oversight.

Mechanically it scans the payment ledger, joins each intent's refunds from the refund ledger, and computes netAmount = chargeAmount − totalRefunded per line plus aggregate totals, giving one concrete, traceable number to hold against the gateway's statement.

Drift between that number and the gateway almost always comes from the seam between two independently-updating systems — a webhook that arrives late or never arrives, a refund that went through on the gateway but whose callback was lost, or the reverse — and none of that is a bug in the arithmetic, just two ledgers momentarily disagreeing about the same real-world event.
Letting the reconciler 'self-heal' by quietly patching the internal figure to match the gateway destroys verifiability — the one property that made the ledger worth having.

Once a number in the books can be silently overwritten, nobody can later tell whether the refund actually happened, why it happened, or whether the fix itself was correct — the drift's root cause is erased along with the evidence.
The correct path keeps detection and correction as two separate responsibilities: the report only surfaces which line is drifting; a human or dedicated compensating job investigates why.
Any correction must be issued as a brand-new ledger entry — with its own id, idempotency key, and timestamp — never an edit to the existing record.
That way every money movement, including the fix, remains an auditable event, and the reconciliation report stays a tool the correction process consumes, never an actor that changes the books itself.

In NestJS, `@Body()` binds the request payload only after the framework's body-parsing pipe has already turned the raw request into a JavaScript object, so by the time a controller sees it, the original wire bytes the client sent no longer exist in that form.

`JSON.stringify()` applied to a parsed object is not guaranteed to reproduce the exact bytes originally transmitted — key enumeration order, number formatting (e.g. `1999` vs `1999.0`), and whitespace/compactness can all differ from whatever serializer the sender used.

An HMAC signature is computed over one specific byte sequence, so verifying it correctly requires hashing that same byte sequence; re-serializing a parsed representation of the payload and hashing that instead produces a different message and therefore a mismatching signature, even when the payload is logically identical to what was sent.

A hand-written test script that signs `JSON.stringify(payload)` and then sends that literal string as the request body will always verify successfully, because the string being hashed and the string being transmitted are identical by construction — this makes the test pass without proving the verification logic is correct.

Because the byte mismatch depends on incidental serialization differences (field order, number formatting) that vary per payload, verification failures appear intermittent and unpredictable in production even though the underlying cause is deterministic and structural.

The fix is to capture the raw, unparsed request body — for example via a framework option like NestJS's `rawBody: true` bootstrap flag — so the original `Buffer` is available for signature verification instead of a re-serialized object.

Signature verification must run against the raw bytes before the body is parsed or trusted for business logic; parsing into a DTO via `@Body()` should only happen after the signature check has passed, never before, so an unverified payload is never acted on.

A correct regression test replays a captured genuine webhook byte-for-byte and expects success, flips a single byte in a copy and expects rejection, and includes a payload whose JSON key order deliberately differs from the parser's default re-serialization order to prove verification no longer depends on re-serialization at all.

The `totalRefunded` helper sums the `amount` field of every refund record in the ledger with no `.filter()` on `status` at all, so a refund the gateway declined contributes to the sum exactly as if it had succeeded.

Tracing the numbers exposes the bug: a captured amount of 2949 with one declined refund attempt of 1000 produces `remaining = 2949 - 1000 = 1949`, even though the declined attempt moved zero dollars — the guard's comparison (`params.amount > remaining`) is correct, the corruption happens entirely inside how `remaining` gets computed.

A declined refund still deserves a `RefundRecord` in the ledger with `status: RefundStatus.Failed` — that part of the design is correct and worth keeping, since a decline is an event worth logging even though no money moved.

The invariant that matters here: only refunds where money actually left the merchant (`status === "succeeded"`) may subtract from the captured amount; a declined attempt is a no-op for the money-movement total regardless of how many records exist for it.

The fix is scoped to `totalRefunded` alone — `refunds.filter((r) => r.status === "succeeded").reduce((sum, r) => sum + r.amount, 0)` — leaving the guard's comparison and the rest of `create` untouched, since the bug was never in how the threshold check itself works.

Recomputing `remaining` from the full refund ledger on every single request, rather than trusting a cached running counter, is what prevents many small partial refunds from ever cumulatively exceeding the captured amount; the fix must preserve this recomputation-on-every-call behavior, only changing which records count toward the sum.

The failure mode is symmetric and equally dangerous in the other direction: if the filter were dropped so nothing counts, or filtered too aggressively so legitimate succeeded refunds get excluded, refunds could exceed the captured total with no guard catching it — the filter has to be exactly `status === "succeeded"`, no broader and no narrower.

Pinning this fix requires four cases: a partial refund that succeeds must reduce `remaining` correctly; a refund attempt that the gateway declines must leave `remaining` unchanged afterward; a refund request for the true remaining balance after that decline must succeed; and a request for one cent more than the true remainder must still be rejected.

A webhook handler can only trust a confirmation once it proves four things about the event: its source (a valid signature from the real gateway), its ownership (which order the reference maps to), its state (whether that order is still in a capturable, non-terminal status), and its value (whether the transferred amount actually matches what is owed) — proving only source and ownership still leaves two exploitable gaps open.

Comparing the incoming transfer amount against the ledger's expected amount is a required guard before a payment can be marked paid; without it, a transfer for less than the order total — as long as it carries the correct reference — still causes the full order to be captured, which is a straightforward underpayment exploit.

When the transferred amount does not match the order amount, the correct behavior is to leave the order matched but still pending for separate reconciliation, not to reject the event outright and not to mark it paid — the order was genuinely found, it just was not paid in full.

Bank and payment-gateway webhook delivery is at-least-once, not exactly-once, so any handler that mutates a ledger on receipt of an event must check whether the order is already in a terminal status before applying the transition again, or a retried/duplicate delivery will silently re-run the same state change.

Without a terminal-state check, a status-only write may look harmless today, but the instant the handler gains any side effect that fires on the transition itself — crediting a wallet, sending a receipt, releasing inventory, calling a downstream capture — every redelivered webhook turns into a duplicate action such as a double-credit or double-capture.

Reviewing a payment webhook handler effectively means walking the guard chain link by link and naming exactly which checks are present and which are missing, rather than commenting on style or naming — the missing links themselves are the finding.

Before approving a change to a payment webhook handler, the reviewer should require tests proving all three outcomes explicitly: an underpaid transfer with a correct reference leaves the order pending, an exact-amount transfer marks the order paid, and delivering the identical webhook event twice results in exactly one transition to paid rather than two.
